examples: I lived in Korea for one year.
nuance: 한국 is the short everyday name for South Korea, while the official long form is 대한민국. People also say 우리나라 when proudly meaning our country.
mistakes: Using 한국 to mean North Korea instead of 북한

examples: My friend lives in the USA.
nuance: 미국 is the standard Korean name for the United States and comes from a Chinese character reading, not from the English sound. It covers the whole country, not just one state.
mistakes: Saying 아메리카 instead of the natural word 미국

examples: I worked in China for two years.
nuance: 중국 is the everyday name for China and the language is 중국어. The country sits right next to Korea, so it appears often in daily talk.
mistakes: Confusing 중국 the country with 중국어 the language

examples: I met a friend in Japan.
nuance: 일본 is the standard name for Japan and the language is 일본어. Many Koreans visit it as a popular nearby travel destination.
mistakes: Mixing up 일본 the country with 일본어 the language

nuance: 영국 refers to the United Kingdom as a whole, not only England. The language English is 영어, a closely related but separate word.
mistakes: Using 영국 to mean only England instead of the UK

examples: I lived in France for one year.
nuance: 프랑스 is written in hangul from the country sound and stays the same in casual or formal speech. The language French is 프랑스어.
mistakes: Spelling it 후랑스 instead of the correct 프랑스

examples: I work at a company in Germany.
nuance: 독일 is the Korean name for Germany and does not sound like the English word. The language German is 독일어, a separate term.
mistakes: Saying 저먼 instead of the natural word 독일

examples: I came to Korea from abroad.
nuance: 외국 means any country other than your own, so it shifts meaning depending on the speaker. A person from a foreign country is called 외국인.
mistakes: Using 외국 when you mean a specific named country

nuance: 나라 is the plain native Korean word for country and works for any nation. Koreans often write 우리나라 as one word to mean our own country warmly.
mistakes: Using 나라 for the abstract noun nation like 국가 in formal writing

nuance: 한국인 means a Korean person using the formal suffix 인, while 한국 사람 is the more casual everyday phrase. Both are correct in polite speech.
mistakes: Saying 한국인 사람, which doubles the meaning of person

examples: I want to travel the world.
I have friends all over the world.
nuance: 세계 means the world as the whole earth and its countries, often paired with 전 to mean the entire world. It is more global in scope than 나라.
mistakes: Confusing 세계 the world with 세상, which means everyday life

examples: My parents live in my hometown.
I go to my hometown on vacation.
nuance: 고향 means the place where you were born and grew up, carrying a warm nostalgic feeling. It can be a city, a town, or a whole region.
mistakes: Using 고향 to mean current home instead of 집
